p.seg: *Féng Yù Piān* (Chapter on Fortuitous Encounters)
*Cāoxíng* (moral conduct) has constant worth,
official careers have inconstant encounters.
Whether one is worthy or unworthy
is a matter of talent;
whether one encounters opportunity or not
is a matter of time.
High talent and pure conduct
cannot guarantee certain honor and nobility;
meager abilities and sullied morals
cannot guarantee certain baseness and lowliness.
Perhaps those with high talent and pure conduct,
If not encountered (by a ruler),
To be relegated to the lower stream;
With meager ability, to muddy one's integrity;
To be favored,
is to be above the masses.
Each age has its own way of selecting scholars,
and scholars also each have their own way of advancing.
Advancement depends on favor,
retreat depends on lack of favor.
To occupy a position of honor and prominence
does not necessarily mean one is virtuous,
it is due to being favored;
to be in a humble position below
does not necessarily mean one is foolish,
it is due to lack of favor.
Therefore, when favored,
one might embrace corrupt conduct
and be more respected than in the court of Jié:
When not favored,
one might uphold pure integrity
and be lower than in the court of Yáo.
The reasons for being favored or not favored
are not uniform:
Sometimes one is truly virtuous but assists evil;
sometimes one uses great talent to follow lesser talent;
sometimes both have great talent, but their paths differ in purity;
sometimes one lacks morals but is suitable due to their skills;
sometimes one lacks skills but gains favor due to their beauty.
Wǔ Yuán, Bó Xǐ,
both served Fūchāi.
Bó Xǐ was respected,
Wǔ Yuán was executed.
This is a case of different conduct under the same ruler.
Or, there are cases of the same conduct under different rulers,
with varying fortune,
Yī Yǐn and Jī Zǐ are examples of this.
Yī Yǐn and Jī Zǐ, their talents were the same,
Yī Yǐn became prime minister,
Jī Zǐ became a slave;
Yī Yǐn met Chéng Tāng,
Jī Zǐ met Shāng Zhòu.
When a worthy serves a worthy ruler,
and the ruler desires to govern well,
the minister assists him with his talent,
their tendencies and preferences coinciding,
their success is naturally appropriate.
When a worthy serves an evil ruler,
and the ruler does not desire to govern well,
the minister assists him with loyal conduct,
their conduct and ambitions clashing,
their failure is naturally appropriate.
Or, sometimes a worthy and sage minister
encounters a ruler who desires to govern well,
yet ultimately meets with misfortune,
Kǒngzǐ and Mèng Kē are examples of this.
Kǒngzǐ ran out of provisions in Chén and Cài,
Mèng Kē was stuck in Qí and Liáng.
It's not that the rulers of those times did not want to use good men,
but that their talent and knowledge were shallow,
and they were unable to employ great talents.
For the one who can control excellent steeds,
must be Wang Liang;
those who can employ Yu, Ji, and Gao Yao as ministers,
must be Yao and Shun.
Using a hand capable of maneuvering within a hundred *li*,
to control feet capable of traveling a thousand *li*,
there will inevitably be the danger of breaking the yoke and snapping the harness;
having the talent to manage common subjects,
and using it to control the wisdom of great ministers,
there will inevitably be a transformation of closed minds and blocked intentions.
Therefore, the most profound words are discarded,
and sages and worthies are resisted,
not because they are hated,
but because the profound words are unpalatable.
Sages and worthies strive for loftiness,
and profound words are difficult to put into practice.
Now, when great talent tries to interact with small talent,
the small talent cannot accept it,
so it is only natural that it is not encountered/accepted.
Or, when a minister of great talent,
encounters a ruler of great talent,
there can still be instances of being encountered or not encountered.
Yú Shùn, Xǔ Yóu, Tàigōng, and Bó Yí are examples of this.
Yú Shùn and
Xǔ Yóu were both sages.
They both lived during the Táng dynasty,
and both were presented before Yáo.
Afterwards, no one recommended him,
yet he still obtained an official position.
Why is that?
Because the omen had already appeared,
and its fulfillment was certain.
In ancient times, years were called *líng* (age),
having already reached nine *líng*,
was like a person dreaming of obtaining a noble rank.
Because Zhōu Gōng took the dream that was sure to come true,
and requested it from Heaven,
how could his merit be small?"
Someone then asked:
"Merit has no large or small,
virtue has no much or little,
people must have someone to look up to and rely on,
then it is good.
If Zhōu Gōng had not substituted for Wǔ Wáng,
and Wǔ Wáng had died of illness,
could Zhōu Gōng and Chéng Wáng have brought about peace and stability to the world?"
He replied:
"It would have been accomplished,
Zhōu Gōng assisted Chéng Wáng and the world would not have been in chaos.
If Wǔ Wáng had not been substituted for,
and consequently died of illness,
is there any doubt that Zhōu Gōng could have brought about peace and stability?"
Someone challenged:
"If that is the case,
Wǔ Wáng's life was of no benefit,
and his death was of no loss,
Zhōu Gōng's merit was necessary for success.
When the Zhōu dynasty declined,
the feudal lords rebelled,
Guǎn Zhòng united the feudal lords nine times,
and rectified the whole world.
Confucius said:
'Without Guǎn Zhòng,
I would be wearing my hair loose and fastening my robes on the left.'
If there had been no Guǎn Zhòng,
and the feudal lords had not been united,
the barbarians would have invaded in waves,
the Central Kingdom would have been annihilated,
this is what the loss of Guǎn Zhòng would have harmed.
Making calculations is beneficial,
the merit of Guǎn Zhòng,
is on par with that of the Duke of Zhou.
When Guǎn Zhòng died,
Duke Huán did not bury him with the rites due to a feudal lord,
comparing him to the Duke of Zhou,
Heaven should have been angry,
why were there no faint thunder and light rain?
Why?
Was it because the Duke of Zhou was a sage while Guǎn Zhòng was not virtuous?
Now, Guǎn Zhòng built a *fǎn diàn*,
and had three returning wives (*sān guī*),
Confucius criticized him for this,
(Someone) thought he was not virtuous.
"Returning the goblet stand,"
"Three Returns,"
are the rites of the feudal lords;
"A Son of Heaven's funeral rites,"
are the regulations of a true king,
all of which, as a subject,
he may not perform.
A great man's virtue aligns with Heaven and Earth.
Confucius,
was a great man,
and he criticized Guǎn Zhòng for overstepping the rites.
(If) Heaven desired Zhōu Gōng's transgression of the regulations,
this is not proof of aligning virtue.
The explanation of the scholars of the *Book of Documents*,
is not acceptable."
To see bird tracks and then know how to write,
to see tumbling weeds and then know how to make a cart,
Heaven did not instruct Cāngjié with bird tracks,
or send Xī Zhòng because of the tumbling weeds.
Xī Zhòng was inspired by the tumbling weeds,
and Cāngjié was inspired by the bird tracks.
When Duke Wén of Jìn returned to his state,
he ordered the removal of the painted chariot,
Jiù Fàn felt deeply moved,
and resigned from his position to return home.
Now, Duke Wén's removal of the painted chariot,
(It was) not that (he) wanted to remove Jiùfàn;
Jiùfàn felt ashamed,
and voluntarily associated himself with the commoners.
Huáchén of Sòng weakened his clan,
and employed six domestic thieves,
who killed Huá Wú with pī-spears behind the zuǒshī (Left Commander) of Sòng at Hé.
The zuǒshī was afraid and said:
"This old man is innocent."
Afterwards, the zuǒshī resented Huáchén,
and Huáchén prepared for him.
The people of the state were chasing a mad dog,
and the mad dog entered the gate of Huáchén's house.
Huáchén thought that the zuǒshī had come to attack him,
and fled over the wall.
Huáchén himself killed Huá Wú, yet the zuǒshī was afraid;
the people of the state themselves chased a mad dog, yet Huáchén himself fled.
The fear of King Chéng,
was similar to this.
He suspected in his heart that he had not buried the Duke with the rites due to the Son of Heaven,
and finally encountered the arrival of thunder and rain,
so he was overly fearful and apprehensive.
The arrival of thunder and rain,
was not necessarily Heaven blaming King Chéng.
The thunder and rain arrived,
and King Chéng was afraid and blamed himself.
To be moved is like the mind of Cāngjié,
or Xīzhòng.
To be fearful is like the zuǒshī,
This is what Huá Chén meant.
Harboring plans of suspicion,
encountering the energy of sudden arrival,
when verification is seen through analogous things,
then the effect of Heaven's anger is achieved.
Seeing verification from similar things in silence and solitude,
one still feels moved and fearful,
how much more so when the thunder and rain raise booming sounds!
Can King Chéng possibly not be frightened?
When there is swift thunder and violent wind,
Kǒng Zǐ certainly changes his countenance.
According to the Rites, when a gentleman hears thunder,
even at night,
he puts on his clothes and cap and sits up,
this is to show respect for the thunder and fear the excited energy.
Sages and gentlemen have no doubt about the Dao,
yet they still follow Heaven's changes and movements,
how much more so when King Chéng suspects Zhōu Gōng,
when he hears the changes of thunder and rain,
how can he not be alarmed and fearful?
Therefore, the arrival of thunder and rain
almost certainly comes from the weather;
King Chéng's fear
almost certainly comes from perceiving the categories of things.
The Dao of Heaven is non-action.
If Heaven uses thunder and rain to angrily rebuke people,
then it can also use thunder and rain to kill the wicked.
Ancient rulers who lacked virtue were many.
If Heaven could punish them with thunder and lightning,
why would it necessarily command sages to raise armies and mobilize troops,
causing armies to be stalled and soldiers to be injured?
If it's difficult to carry out punishment with a single thunderbolt,
and easy to defeat enemies with three armies,
why would Heaven not be afraid of trouble?
Someone might say:
"Zhòu's 紂 father, Dì Yǐ 帝乙,
shot at the sky and beat the ground,
roaming between the Hé 河 and
Wèi 渭 Rivers,
and was struck and killed by thunder and lightning.
This is Heaven punishing the wicked with thunder and lightning."
But the evil of Dì Yǐ 帝乙,
compared to that of Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂,
Zōu Bóqí 鄒伯奇 argued that the evil of Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂 was not as great as that of the fallen Qín 秦,
and the fallen Qín 秦 was not as great as that of Wáng Mǎng 王莽.
However, the deaths of Jié 桀, Zhòu 紂, Qín 秦, and Mǎng 莽
did not involve thunder and lightning.
Confucius, in writing the *Chūnqiū 春秋* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
selected even the slightest good,
and disparaged even the tiniest evil,
selecting good without exaggerating its beauty,
and disparaging evil without exceeding its transgression.
To blame a small thing with great consequence
no man will do.
King Chéngwáng 成王 had a small doubt,
To blame the small with the standard of the great,
no one does that.
King Chéng had a small doubt,
and heaven responded with great thunder and rain.
If even the burial of a duke by his subject can be settled,
what change could exceed this?
The "Hóng Fàn" investigates doubts,
but those who don't understand calamities and changes
simply lack the ability to fully comprehend them.
Heaven doesn't blame people for not being able to resolve every doubt.
King Chéng's heart was hesitant and unresolved,
and heaven blamed him with great thunder and rain.
That probably wasn't the intention of Imperial Heaven.
The interpretations of the "Book" scholars
probably miss the truth.
The "Qí Shì Piān"
says that people of the upper ages
were large and tall, fine and handsome,
strong and long-lived,
living to be around a hundred years old;
people of the lower ages
are short and small, ugly and deformed,
and die young and prematurely.
Why is this?
The upper ages had harmonious and pure atmospheres,
marriages occurred at the proper time,
and the people were born with good qi,
Being born without injury,
with firm bones and joints,
therefore one grows up to a long and healthy old age,
with a beautiful appearance.
The opposite is true in later generations,
therefore one is short, small, and dies young,
with an ugly appearance.
This is a false statement.
Those who governed in earlier ages were sages (shèngrén),
were also sages (shèngrén).
Those who governed in later ages
were also sages (shèngrén).
The virtue of sages (shèngrén),
does not differ from past to present,
therefore their governance of the world
is no different from ancient to modern times.
The heaven of earlier ages
is the heaven of later ages,
Heaven does not change,
and the qi (qì) does not alter.
The people of earlier ages
are the people of later ages,
all endowed with primordial qi (yuánqì).
Primordial qi (yuánqì) is pure and harmonious,
and has not differed from ancient to modern times,
therefore those who are endowed with it to form their bodies,
why are they different?
If their received *qi* is equal,
then their inherent nature will be uniform.
If their inherent nature is uniform,
then their physical forms will be the same.
If their physical forms are the same,
then ugliness and beauty will be equal.
If ugliness and beauty are equal,
then premature death and long life will be appropriate.
One heaven and one earth
together produce myriad things.
The birth of myriad things
all receive one *qi*.
The thinness or thickness of this *qi*,
is seemingly the same for ten thousand generations.
Emperors govern the world,
for a hundred generations they follow the same path.
The people marry,
observing the same rites at the same time,
although it is said that men marry at thirty,
and women marry at twenty,
legal regulations are established,
but they are not necessarily followed.
How can we verify this?
Because they are not followed today.
The system of ritual and music
exists and is seen today,
but do the people of today
willingly practice them?
Modern people are unwilling to practice it,
and the ancients were also unwilling to promote it.
Using the people of today
to understand the people of ancient times.
People
are things,
and things are also things.
A person lives in the world
to a life span of one hundred years.
When one is born as a ten-year-old child,
of the things seen on the earth,
many undergo birth, death, change, and alteration.
As for reaching one hundred years,
when one is about to die,
the various things seen
are no different from what one saw at the age of ten.
There is no difference.
If those in the upper generations and the lower generations,
the people are not different,
then the time between one hundred years
is enough to divine the future.
The height and size of the six domestic animals,
the size of the five grains,
insects, grasses, and trees,
gold, stones, pearls, and jade,
tiny flying and wriggling creatures,
those that crawl and those that breathe with a beak,
無有異者， There is nothing different.
此形不異也。 This form is not different.
古之水火、 The water and fire of ancient times,
今之水火也。 are the water and fire of today.
今氣為水火也， Today's *qì* becomes water and fire.
使氣有異， If the *qì* were different,
則古之水清火熱， then would the water of ancient times be clear and the fire hot,
而今水濁火寒乎？ and the water of today be turbid and the fire cold?
人生長六七尺， A person is born and grows to six or seven *chǐ*,
大三四圍， with a girth of three or four *wéi*,
面有五色， a face with five colors,
壽至於百， and a lifespan reaching a hundred years—
萬世不異。 for ten thousand generations, this is not different.
如以上世人民， If the people of previous ages
侗長佼好， were exceptionally tall and beautiful,
堅彊老壽， strong and long-lived,
下世反此， and later generations were the opposite,
則天地初立， then when heaven and earth were first established,
始為人時， when people first came into being,
長可如Fángfēng zhī Jūn, could their height have been like that of the lord of Fángfēng,
色如Sòng Cháo， their complexion like Sòng Cháo,
壽如Péngzǔ乎？ their lifespan like Péngzǔ's?
從當今至千世之後， From the present day to a thousand generations hence,
人可長如莢英， could people be as tall as a *jiá yīng* (small pod),
色如Mómǔ， their complexion like Mómǔ's,
壽如朝生乎？ their lifespan like that of a morning glory?
Wáng Mǎng之時， During the time of Wáng Mǎng,
長人生長一丈， a very tall person was one *zhàng* tall,
名曰霸出。 míng yuē Bà Chū. It is named "Bà Chū."
建武年中， Jiànwǔ nián zhōng, During the Jiànwǔ reign period (25-56 AD),
潁川張仲師長二尺二寸。 Yǐngchuān Zhāng Zhòngshī zhǎng èr chǐ èr cùn. Zhāng Zhòngshī of Yǐngchuān was two chi and two cun tall.
張湯八尺有餘， Zhāng Tāng bā chǐ yǒuyú, Zhāng Tāng was over eight chi tall,
其父不滿五尺。 qí fù bù mǎn wǔ chǐ. while his father was less than five chi.
俱在今世， jū zài jīnshì, Both are alive in the present age.
或長或短， huò cháng huò duǎn, Some are tall, some are short.
儒者之言， Rúzhě zhī yán, The words of the Confucian scholars
竟非誤也。 jìng fēi wù yě. are not at all mistaken.
語稱上世使民以宜， yǔ chēng shàngshì shǐ mín yǐ yí, It is said that in ancient times, people were employed according to their suitability;
傴者抱關， yǔ zhě bào guān, hunchbacks guarded the gates,
侏儒俳優。 zhūrú pāiyōu. and dwarfs were performers.
如皆侗長佼好， rú jiē tóng cháng jiǎo hǎo, If everyone were tall and handsome,
安得傴、 ān dé yǔ, where would one get the hunchbacks
侏之人乎？ zhū zhī rén hū? and dwarfs?
語稱上世之人， yǔ chēng shàngshì zhī rén, It is said that the people of ancient times
質朴易化； zhìpǔ yì huà; were simple and easy to transform;
下世之人， xiàshì zhī rén, but the people of later ages
文薄難治。 wén bó nán zhì. are cultured but shallow and difficult to govern.
故《易》曰： gù "Yì" yuē: Therefore, the *Book of Changes* says:
「上古之時結繩以治， "shànggǔ zhī shí jié shéng yǐ zhì, "In ancient times, knots were tied in ropes to govern;
後世易之以書契。」 hòushì yì zhī yǐ shūqì." later generations replaced them with written contracts."
先結繩， xiān jié shéng, First there were knotted ropes;
易化之效； yì huà zhī xiào; this was evidence of ease of transformation.
後書契， hòu shūqì, Later there were written contracts;
難治之驗也。 nán zhì zhī yàn yě. this was proof of the difficulty of governing.
故夫宓犧之前， gù fū Mìxī zhī qián, Therefore, before Fúxī,
The people were most simple and genuine.
Those who slept, rested comfortably;
those who sat, sat leisurely.
They lived in groups and gathered together,
knowing their mothers but not recognizing their fathers.
By the time of Fúxī,
the people had become somewhat refined,
knowing to use cunning to deceive the foolish,
the brave wanting to intimidate the timid,
the strong wanting to bully the weak,
the many wanting to tyrannize the few.
Therefore, Fúxī created the Eight Trigrams (bāguà) to govern them.
By the time of the Zhōu dynasty,
the people's refinement was shallow,
and the Eight Trigrams were difficult to reiterate and follow.
Therefore, King Wén expanded them into sixty-four hexagrams,
exhausting their permutations,
so that the people would not grow weary.
By the time of the Zhōu dynasty,
the people had long been shallow,
so Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) wrote the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
selecting the slightest goodness,
denouncing the smallest evil,
saying:
"Zhōu (The Zhōu dynasty) observed the preceding two dynasties,
how rich and flourishing in culture!
I follow Zhōu."
Kǒngzǐ knew that the world was gradually deteriorating,
When culture is shallow, it is difficult to govern.
Therefore, (people) add layers of dense netting,
establishing extremely fine prohibitions,
employing checks and balances to maintain control,
with preparations complete and thorough.
These words are nonsense.
The people of ancient times
cherished the Five Constant Virtues;
the people of later times
also cherished the Five Constant Virtues.
Both cherish the Way of the Five Constant Virtues,
both are born receiving the same vital energy;
so how is it that ancient times were simple and unadorned?
How is it that later times are cultured and shallow?
Those people see that the people of ancient times
drank blood and ate fur,
without the food of the five grains.
Later generations dug wells into the earth,
cultivated the soil and planted grains,
drinking well water and eating millet,
with the tempering of water and fire;
they also see that in high antiquity, people lived in caves and nests,
wearing the skins of birds and beasts.
Later generations exchanged these for palaces and houses,
with adornments of cloth and silk.
Then they say that ancient times were simple and unadorned,
and later times were cultured and shallow.
夫 qì yè biàn yì,
while innate nature and conduct do not differ.
However, there are expressions like "simplicity" and "elegance,"
because the world experiences prosperity and decline.
Extreme decline inevitably leads to corruption.
shuāi jí jiǔ yǒu bì yě.
It is like clothing and food for people:
when first made, they are fresh and complete;
when first ripe, they are fragrant and clean;
after a short time, they are worn and torn;
after a few days, they are stinky and rotten.
The principles of elegance and substance
are shared by ancient and modern times.
One substance and one elegance,
one decline and one prosperity—
these existed in ancient times;
it's not unique to the present.
How can we verify this?
The *Commentary* says:
"The kings of the Xià Hòu Shì Dynasty taught with loyalty.
The superiors taught with loyalty,
and the gentlemen were loyal,
but the failing was that
the common people became unrefined.
To remedy unrefinedness, nothing is better than reverence.
The kings of the Yīn Dynasty taught with reverence.
The superiors taught with reverence,
and the gentlemen were reverent,
but the failing was that
the common people became superstitious.
To remedy superstition, nothing is better than elegance.
Therefore, the kings of the Zhōu Dynasty taught with elegance.
The superiors taught with elegance,
and gentlemen are refined,
the fault lies in that
the common person is unfeeling.
To remedy this unfeelingness, nothing is better than loyalty."
Those who succeed the Zhōu dynasty and become rulers,
should teach loyalty.
The Xià dynasty, which succeeded the teachings of Táng
and Yú, found them to be unfeeling,
therefore they taught loyalty.
If Táng and Yú taught refinement,
then those whom they succeeded must have lost their way in ghostliness.
When people see that refinement in the present day is unfeeling,
and they treat it with familiarity and scorn it,
they then say that the ancient world was simple and genuine,
and that the later world is refined and unfeeling,
it is like when family members are not careful,
one then says that the children of other families are careful and good.
The saying is that people of ancient times
valued righteousness and lightly regarded their own lives.
When they encountered matters of loyalty and righteousness,
and it was clear that they should give their lives,
則 bì fù tāng qū fēng, [then certainly they would rush into boiling water and towards sharp blades,]
sǐ bù gù hèn. [even dying without regard for resentment.]
Gù Hóng Yǎn zhī jié, [Therefore, the integrity of Hóng Yǎn,]
Chén Bùzhàn zhī yì, [the righteousness of Chén Bùzhàn,]
xíngshì bǐlèi, [examples of such actions, compared and classified,]
shūjí suǒ zài, [are recorded in books,]
wángmìng juān shēn, [sacrificing life and donating oneself,]
zhòngduō fēi yī. [are numerous, not just one.]
Jīnshì qū lì gǒu shēng, [Nowadays, people pursue profit and seek a wretched existence,]
qì yì wàng dé, [abandoning righteousness and recklessly seeking gain,]
bù xiāng miǎn yǐ yì, [not encouraging each other with righteousness,]
bù xiāng jī yǐ xíng, [nor spurring each other on with action,]
yì fèi shēn bù yǐ wéi lěi, [righteousness is abandoned, and they do not consider it a burden,]
xíng huī shì bù yǐ xiāng wèi. [action is ruined, and they do not fear each other.]
Cǐ yán wàng yě. [This is a reckless statement.]
Fú shàngshì zhī shì, [Now, the gentlemen of ancient times,]
jīnshì zhī shì yě, [and the gentlemen of today,]
jù hán rényì zhī xìng, [both possess the nature of benevolence and righteousness,]
zé qí zāo shì, [then, when they encounter affairs,]
bìng yǒu fèn shēn zhī jié. [they all have the integrity to devote themselves.]
Gǔ yǒu wúyì zhī rén, [In ancient times, there were unrighteous people,]
jīn yǒu jiàn jié zhī shì, [and today, there are gentlemen who establish integrity.]
Shàn'è zázè, [Good and evil are mixed,]
hé shì wú yǒu? [what age does not have them?]
Shùshì zhě hào gāo gǔ ér xià jīn, [Those who narrate affairs admire the high antiquity and disparage the present,]
guì suǒ wén ér jiàn suǒ jiàn. [value what they have heard and disdain what they have seen.]
Biàn shì zé tán qí jiǔ zhě, [Orators talk about what is old,]
Wénrén zé zhù qí yuǎn zhě. Literary men then record those who are distant (in time).

Now, not understanding the origin of accumulative harm

"Chapter on Fate and Fortune"
That ordinary people encounter chance and suffer burdens and harms
is all due to fate.
There is the fate of life and death, longevity and early demise,
and there is also the fate of nobility and lowliness, poverty and wealth.
From princes and dukes down to commoners,
sages and the most foolish,
all who have heads and eyes,
and belong to the blood-containing category,
none do not have fate.
If fate decrees poverty and lowliness,
even if one is enriched and ennobled,
they will still encounter misfortune and lose their wealth and nobility;
if fate decrees wealth and nobility,
even if one is impoverished and lowly,
they will still encounter good fortune and escape their poverty and lowliness.
Therefore, those with a noble fate
rise from humble beginnings,
while those with a lowly fate
are endangered from positions of wealth.
Thus, wealth and nobility seem to have divine assistance,
while poverty and lowliness seem to have ghostly misfortune.
People with a noble fate,
all learn and uniquely succeed,
and are uniquely promoted in official service;
people with a wealthy fate,
all seek and uniquely obtain,
and all uniquely achieve.
Poverty and lowliness are the opposite,
difficult to succeed, difficult to be promoted,
difficult to obtain, difficult to achieve;
To obtain past transgressions and receive punishment,
to have illness cause loss and abandonment,
to lose one's wealth and status,
is to be poor and lowly.
Therefore, to have high talent and profound conduct
does not necessarily guarantee one will be rich and noble.
To have little wisdom and thin virtue

Sometimes, to have high talent and profound conduct,

To have little wisdom and thin virtue,
but a good fate,

Therefore, in facing matters, knowing foolishness,

Officialdom being noble or lowly,

Fate cannot be forced,

The wise attribute it to Heaven,

Making wealth and status like digging a ditch and chopping firewood,
adding an effort to strive,
To achieve a state of strength and vigor,

If even those without destiny

However, it is possible that the ditch is not yet cleared but encounters a flood,

Not becoming a high official,

Having talent but not being able to employ it,

When people in the world see someone with high moral conduct,

When they see someone with deep planning and consideration,

Nobility and wealth are due to destiny, fortune, and prosperity;
It does not depend on the worthy, the wise, eloquence, or intelligence.

"Wealth cannot be obtained through calculation or strategy,

Wearing silver seals and purple ribbons [i.e., holding high office],

Sometimes, the lowly and foolish amass a thousand gold pieces,

Therefore, officials of the same talent

Fortune and destiny determine poverty and wealth;

Nature and destiny determine nobility and lowliness;

The talent of King Chéng (成王) was not as great as that of the Duke of Zhōu (周公);

Therefore, nobility and lowliness are determined by fate,

Ordinary people's appointed fates are of two kinds:
first, the fate of what one is destined to encounter;
second, the fate of strength and weakness, longevity and premature death.
What one is destined to encounter
refers to death by weapons, burning, crushing, or drowning;
strength and longevity, weakness and premature death
refer to the thickness or thinness of the qi one is endowed with.
Death by weapons, burning, crushing, or drowning depends on the endowment one has as fate;
there is necessarily no fixed time for it.
As for strength and weakness, premature death and longevity, a hundred is taken as the standard;
those who do not reach a hundred
are naturally deficient in qi.
If the endowment of qi is thick, then the body is strong;
if the body is strong, then its lifespan is long;
if the qi is thin, then the body is weak;
if the body is weak, then its lifespan is short;
if the lifespan is short, then there are many illnesses
and short lifespans.
Dying shortly after birth,
or being injured before delivery,
is due to a thin and weak endowment;
people with a thick and strong endowment will certainly complete their allotted lifespan.
As for those who have no encounters,
live idly in impoverished conditions,
and die of shortness of breath,
this is because their endowment is thin
and they have exhausted its use.
To fully attain what one aspires to in one's heart is rare.
"Chapter on the Formless"
People receive primordial qi from Heaven,
each receiving a destiny of longevity or premature death,
to establish a long or short form,
just as potters use clay to make round sacrificial vessels (guǐ) and angled eaves (lián wǔ),
and metalworkers use copper to make trays (pán) and tubs (yú).
Once the shape of the vessel is formed,
it cannot be made smaller or larger;
once the human body is determined,
it cannot be decreased or increased.
Using qi as nature,
when nature is formed, destiny is set.
The body's qi and physical form embrace each other,
life and death depend on their appointed times.
Form cannot be changed,
destiny cannot be reduced or added to.
Speaking in terms of pottery and metalworking,
the length of human life
can be discussed.
Someone might object, saying:
When potters use clay to make round sacrificial vessels (guǐ) and angled eaves (lián wǔ),
once the round sacrificial vessels and angled eaves are formed,
they eventually break and are ruined,
and cannot be changed back.
But when metalworkers use copper to make trays (pán) and tubs (yú), even though the trays and tubs
have become vessels,
It can still be melted again,
a shallow dish can be made into a *zūn* vessel,
but a *zūn* vessel cannot be made into a *guǐ* vessel.
Humans receive their *qì* from Heaven,
and although each receives a destiny of lifespan and premature death,
establishing themselves with a physical form,
if they obtain good methods and divine medicines,
their form can be transformed,
and their lifespan can be increased.
Someone said:
When smelters transform and change things into vessels,
they must first use fire to burn and melt them,
then they can be made large, small, short, or long.
People hope to prolong their years,
and wish to be like bronze vessels,
they should have a transformation similar to a furnace and charcoal,
then their form will be changed;
if their form is changed,
their lifespan can also be increased.
How can people transform their form,
and be like bronze vessels melted by fire?
The *Lǐ* (Book of Rites) says:
"When floods descend,
do not offer fish and turtles."
Why?
Because when rainwater violently falls,
worms and snakes transform,
to transform into fish and turtles.
Separated from their original true forms, they become transient insects.
As ministers are cautious,
therefore, they dare not offer them.
People desire transformation of their bodies,
hoping for a change like insects and snakes?
Now, insects and snakes that haven't transformed,
are not as good as those that haven't transformed.
Insects and snakes that haven't transformed,
people don't eat;
transformed into fish and turtles,
people then eat them.
Being eaten means their lifespan is shortened,
which is not what's hoped for.
As time goes by,
the weather changes the types of things,
toads become quails,
sparrows become clams.
People desire transformation of their bodies,
hoping for something like quails and clams, fish and turtles?
People set traps for clams,
those who catch them eat them.
Even if the body doesn't transform,
lifespan cannot be extended,
which is not what's hoped for.
Gōng of Lǔ, Niú Āi, was bedridden with illness,
and after seven days, he transformed into a tiger;
Gǔn was executed on Yǔshān,
To transform into a yellow bear-like creature,
those who wish to transform their bodies,
hoping to be like Niú Āi becoming a tiger,
or Gǔn becoming a bear-like creature?
Then, even the lifespan of a tiger or bear-like creature
cannot surpass that of a human.
In the nature of Heaven and Earth,
humans are the most noble.
To change the form of a human,
and instead become a bird or beast,
is not something to be hoped for.
What can be hoped for
is an old man transforming into an infant,
secondly, white hair turning black again,
fallen teeth growing back,
a body and spirit strong and vigorous,
riding high without decline;
that is what is valuable.
Merely changing the form,
without extending lifespan,
what benefit is there in that?
Moreover, the transformation of things follows the *qi*,
as if responding to governance,
having some symbolic purpose;
it is not because Heaven desires longevity
that it changes their form.
It is also not because one obtains divine herbs or precious medicines
and eats them and thus transforms.
People constantly take medicine to solidify longevity,
which can increase their original nature
and benefit their lifespan.
Encountering temporal changes
is not the proper *qi* of Heaven,
nor the true nature received by people.
Heaven and earth do not change,
the sun and moon do not alter,
the stars and planets do not disappear,
these are proper.
People receive proper *qi*,
therefore their bodies do not change.
At times men are transformed into women,
women are transformed into men,
high banks become valleys,
and deep valleys become hills,
these are transformations responding to the government,
changes because of the government,
they are not the constant nature.
When the Hàn dynasty rose,
an old man gave Zhāng Liáng a book,
which later transformed into stone;
therefore, the essence of the stone
was an auspicious omen for the rise of the Hàn.
Similarly, the essence of the Yellow River had a person
hold a jade disc and give it to the Qín envoy,
which was a sign of the Qín's demise.
Silkworms eat mulberry leaves until they are old,
The silk spun becomes a cocoon,
the cocoon then transforms into a moth,
the moth has two wings,
changing and departing from the silkworm's form.
The grub transforms into a fùyù (a beetle larva),
the fùyù turns into a cicada,
the cicada grows two wings,
unlike the grub.
All creatures that wriggle and fly,
mostly change their forms,
alter their bodies;
the perfected person alone does not change,
because they are endowed with correctness.
Born as an infant,
growing into a man,
aging into an old father,
from birth to death,
never changing,
this is natural.
Those whose nature does not change,
cannot be made to change again;
those who change,
cannot be made not to change.
As for the lifespan of those who change,
it is not as long as those who do not change.
If people wish to change their form,
then they should increase their years,
this is acceptable.
If one merely changes one's form, but one's lifespan doesn't increase,
then one is like a cicada.
Why would people desire that?
The dragon, being a creature,
sometimes exists and sometimes vanishes,
sometimes is short and sometimes is long.
The nature of the dragon is such that
changes happen in an instant,
and it constantly returns to being extraordinary.
From this perspective,
humans are things
that receive an unchanging form,
a form that cannot be altered,
and a lifespan that cannot be increased or decreased.
The *Zhuan* states that Gāo Zōng 高宗 experienced the anomaly of a mulberry tree and a grain tree growing together.
He repented his errors and reversed his policies,
enjoying a hundred years of happiness.
This is false.
The *Zhuan* says that Sòng Jǐng Gōng 宋景公 uttered three good words,
and the planet Mars retreated three *shè* (houses of the zodiac),
extending his life by twenty-one years.
This is also false.
It also states that Qín Mù Gōng 秦繆公 had evident virtue,
and God on High granted him nineteen years.
This is also false.
It claims that Chì Sōng 赤松 and Wáng Qiáo 王喬, who loved the Dao, became immortals,
crossing over the world without dying.

Suppose a person is born and takes on a form, called "A,"

Indeed, the physical form cannot be changed,

Form, qi, and nature

Form is like spring,

If the qi and nature are not in balance,

An ox's lifespan is half that of a horse,

Therefore, the form of an ox or horse is different from that of a person.
Receiving the form of an ox or horse,

If an ox or horse does not transform into a person,
then its lifespan will also be shorter than that of a person.
The world speaks of the followers of Gāo Zōng,

Therefore, there are beliefs about it.
The blood and qi of the body are
like grain stored in a bag.
If the grain is one *shí*,
the height and size of the bag will also fit one *shí*.
If the grain is increased or decreased,
the bag will also increase or decrease.
People use qi as their lifespan;
qi is like grain,
and the body is like the bag.
If one's lifespan is increased or decreased,
one's body should also increase or decrease.
How can the body remain as it was?
If you say that a person's form is different from a bag,

The juice of the calabash
is like a person's blood;
its flesh
is like meat.
Try to have someone increase or decrease the juice of a calabash,
and make its form stay the same;
could they endure doing this?
People cannot endure increasing or decreasing the juice of a calabash,
how can Heaven endure increasing or decreasing a person's years?
A person's years cannot be increased or decreased.
The followers of Gāo Zōng, who increased it?
Yet they claim it was increased.
If you say the followers of Gāo Zōng
Only if the form and body change,
will its years also increase,
can that be believed.
Now, it is said that years increase,
but it is not said that its body changes,
that is not believable.
Why is that?
People receive qi from heaven,
when qi forms then the body is established,
then fate and form rely on each other, until death,
the form cannot be changed,
nor can the years be increased.
How can this be verified?
When people are alive they can walk,
when they die they become stiff and fall,
when they die, the qi is extinguished,
the form disappears and decays.
Having received qi to be born as a human, the form
cannot be changed,
how can its years increase?
From life to old age,
that which changes on the body
is hair and skin.
When people are young, their hair is black,
when old, their hair is white,
after being white for a long time, it becomes yellow.
The change of hair,
is not a change of form.
When people are young, their skin is fair;
when they are old, their skin is dark;
after being dark for a long time, it becomes dull,
as if it were covered in grime.
The hair turns yellow and the skin becomes grime-like;
therefore the *Lǐ* (Book of Rites) says:
"Huáng gǒu wú jiāng" (May your yellow hair and mottled skin have no end).
The hair and skin change and become different;
therefore, when people are old, they live long and die late.
Bones and flesh cannot be changed;
when life reaches its limit, one dies.
Among the things of the Five Elements,
what can be changed
is only earth.
It can be molded into horses,
changed into people;
this is called "not yet entering the potter's kiln to undergo fire."
If it were made into a vessel,
entering the kiln and undergoing fire,
it would be firm and hard, unable to be changed again.
Now people think that [human bodies] are forged by Heaven and Earth;
the form has already been fixed,
how can it be changed again?
They draw the forms of immortals;
their bodies grow hair,
their arms transform into wings,
they walk on clouds, and their years increase;

This is a false illustration.
In the world, there are false words,

Assuming they are real,

Among the thirty-five countries overseas,
there are the Máomín (毛民, Hairy People) and Yǔmín (羽民, Feathered People).
羽 (yǔ) means wings.
These 毛羽之民 (máoyǔ zhī mín, people with feathers and hair),

Yǔ (禹) and Yì (益) saw the Xī Wángmǔ (西王母, Queen Mother of the West),

The immortal people
are also in foreign lands,
but it is not said they have feathers and hair.
As for the people with feathers and hair,
it is not said they are immortal;
as for the immortal people,
it is not said they have feathers and hair.
Feathers and hair cannot be used to imitate immortality.
If immortals have wings,
how can this be sufficient to prove longevity?
The "Shuàixìng Piān (率性篇, Following Nature Chapter)"
discusses human nature,
asserting that it is definitively both good and evil.
Those who are good
are inherently good.
As for those who are evil,
they can certainly be taught, admonished, and urged
to become good.
All rulers and fathers
should carefully observe the nature of their subjects and children.
If they are good, then nurture and encourage them,
not allowing them to approach evil.
If they approach evil, then assist and protect them, forbidding and preventing them,
so that they gradually turn to good.
Good gradually turns into evil,
evil transforms into good,
and it becomes their inherent nature and conduct.
Zhào Gōng (召公) admonished Chéng Wáng (成王), saying:
"Now Your Majesty is newly receiving your mandate.
Alas!
It is like a newborn child, nothing is not dependent on its initial birth."
"Newborn child" refers to the fifteen sons.
If the initial intention leans toward good,
it will end with good;
if the initial intention leans toward evil,
it will end with evil.
The *Shī* (詩) [Book of Odes] says:
"That beautiful person,
with what shall I associate with them?"
The *Zhuàn* (傳) [Commentary] says:
"It's like refining silk,

A fifteen-year-old child is like that silk.
Their gradual transformation into good or evil

causing it to become blue or red.
Once blue or red is formed,
the true color is no different.
Therefore, Yángzǐ 楊子 wept at the crossroads,
Mòzǐ 墨子 wept at the refined silk.
They grieved over being separated from the original state,
which cannot be changed back.
Human nature,
good can be transformed into evil,
evil can be transformed into good,
it's like this analogy.
Wormwood growing among hemp,
it straightens without support;
white silk entering black cloth,
it becomes black without dyeing.
The nature of wormwood is not straight,
the substance of silk is not black,
the hemp supports, the black cloth dyes,
causing them to be straight and black.
Human nature
is like wormwood and silk,
depending on what it is gradually influenced by, it transforms into good or evil.
Wáng Liáng, Zào Fù are called skilled charioteers,

If they could only drive good horses,

Therefore it is said:
"When Wáng Liáng mounts the chariot,

The *Commentary* says:
"The people of Yáo and Shùn

"These people,
are what made the Three Dynasties able to follow the correct path."
The people of a sage ruler are like that,
the people of an evil ruler are like this,

Those who hear of Bó Yí's influence,

those who hear of Liǔxià Huì's influence,

Just hearing of their reputation
Yóu huò biànjié,

The seventy disciples of Confucius,

were imbued with the teachings of the sages,
their literary talents were refined,
and their knowledge and abilities were tenfold [improved],
due to the merit of instruction and the power of gradual influence.
Before entering the gate of Confucius,

The one who was most unwilling to be led was

The world called Zǐlù an ordinary man without constancy.
Before entering the gate of Confucius,

hearing the sound of reciting,

Confucius led him and taught him,

opening, guiding, and advancing him,

Now, fertility and barrenness are the inherent nature of land.
tǔ dì zhī běn xìng yě.
Land that is fertile and rich is inherently good, and the trees and crops grow abundantly.
shù jià fēng mào;
Land that is barren and infertile is inherently bad, but if one plows deeply and hoes finely,
shēn gēng xì chú,

The height of the land

If one digs the land with picks and shovels,

If one continues to add picks and shovels,

If human nature can be good or bad,

Goodness, through transforming influence,
cultivates its education and instruction,

善 zé qiě gèng yí
turn back and be better than the previous good.
It is like adding picks and shovels when digging low ground,
which is even more effective than working on high ground.
"Sì did not accept fate, but engaged in commerce."
Sì originally did not accept the heaven's decree of wealth. What he added

Those who become wealthy people in the world

If one obtains the skill,
even without accepting fate,

A person with an evil nature

The likes of Táng Xī and Yú Cháng,

their original blocks

Try taking a sword worth only one gold piece from the East,
Further refine and temper,
supply sufficient fire,

Now, natural iron and stone

Why worry about the evil in human nature?

A person's wrongdoing

In the Way of Heaven, there is truth and falsehood.

Now, regarding a person with an evil nature,

The Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) and the Flame Emperor (Yándì) contended to be the Son of Heaven,

Yao (Yáo) yielded the empire to Shun (Shùn),

Even though birds and beasts have different forms from humans,

Extending this to argue,

Different kinds become the same because of their differences,

All those who possess blood and breath

The people of the four states,

Now, those whose nature is evil,

In the traces of gentlemen,

三軍之士，
cannot be controlled [simply by force];

Fire,
and blades, are not things that human nature desires,

It's like the five grains, all are useful,
In reality they are not different, but their effects are different,

The cruel receives

*Ōuhuì Piān* ("Chapter on Coincidence")
Fate,
is the master of fortune and misfortune.

the number of chance encounters;

could suppress or move it

Chén shì wèi chán,

two coincidences and three confluences,

It was on behalf of two rulers that they emerged.

Chapter on Original Nature
Emotions and nature,
Are the foundation of human governance,
From which ritual and music arise.
Therefore, examining the extremes of emotions and nature,
Ritual is used as a preventative measure,
music is used as a means of restraint.
Because human nature contains humility, deference, and yielding,
ritual is created to fit its appropriateness;
because emotions contain likes, dislikes, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure,
music is created to express reverence.
The means by which ritual controls,
and the reason music is created,
are emotion and nature.
In the past, scholars and former students

Shì Shuò of the Zhōu dynasty

Elevating the good nature of people,

Therefore, Shìzǐ composed the chapter "Yǎng Shū" (Nurturing the Nature).
Mì Zǐjiàn, Qī Diāo Kāi,
and the disciples of Gōngsūn Nízi,

Accompanying the heir apparent in and out,

This is what is meant by saying that human life has no high or low status.

"Essay on the Nature of Things"
Scholars of Confucianism argue:
"Heaven and earth intentionally produce humans."
This statement is absurd.
For heaven and earth combine their vital energies,
and humans are produced spontaneously;
just as husband and wife combine their vital energies,
and children are produced spontaneously.
Husband and wife combine their vital energies,
not because they intentionally want to produce a child at that moment,
but because their emotions and desires move them to unite,
and uniting results in the birth of a child.
Furthermore, husband and wife do not intentionally produce children,
which shows that heaven and earth do not intentionally produce humans.
Therefore, humans are born from heaven and earth,
like fish in a pool,
or lice on a person,
arising from vital energies,
and reproducing within their kind.
The myriad things born between heaven and earth,
are all one reality.
The Commentary says:
「Tiāndì bù gù shēng rén,
humans arose spontaneously by chance."
If that is so,
why do those who discuss matters say: "Heaven and earth are the furnace,
the myriad things are the copper,
yin and yang are the fire,
and creation is the craftsman"?
Now, the potter's use of fire
melts copper and bakes vessels,
that is why he does it;
but if you say, "Heaven and earth did not intentionally create humans,
humans arose spontaneously by chance,"
can it be said that the potter
does not intentionally make vessels,
but the vessels are formed spontaneously by chance?
If the analogy does not fit the matter,
it cannot be called an analogy;
if the writing does not match the reality,
it cannot be called correct.
He says:
This is an analogy for people receiving *qi*
that is not completely pure and uniform,
like the casting of copper results in different shapes,
and the firing of vessels depends on how they get the fire,
it is not saying that heaven and earth creating people
is the same as pottery.
In making analogies,
People all speak of human affairs.
Human affairs have an inherent structure,
which cannot be severed.
If you look at the head with your eyes,
the head cannot help but move;
if you join the hands with the feet,
the feet cannot help but sway.
The eyes and the head share the same form,
the hands and the feet share the same body.
Now, consider the potter:
when he first molds the clay to make vessels,
he must use molds to give them shape;
this is done intentionally.
When burning charcoal to generate fire,
he must adjust and harmonize the furnace;
this is also done intentionally.
But even when smelting copper, it cannot all be perfectly formed;
when firing pottery, it cannot all be perfectly good;
this is because intentionality has its limits.
If even Heaven cannot intentionally create people,
