A (gentle)man
must certainly be consistent in this matter."
Mèngzǐ said,
"Both are right.
When I was in Sòng,
I was about to travel far.
Travelers must have parting gifts.
I declined, saying,
'Return the parting gifts.'
Why would I not accept it?
When I was in Xuē,
I had a wary heart,
and my refusal said:
"I heard of the reward,
so perhaps it was for precautions against war and preparations for returning home!"
Why shouldn't I accept it?
If I were in Qí,
then I would have nowhere to place it.
To have nowhere to place it and yet return it,
is to treat it as merchandise.
How could there be a junzi that can be acquired through merchandise?"
Regarding the return of gold,
whether one accepts it or does not accept it,
there are reasons for both.
It is not that one is greedy when one accepts it,
or that one is not greedy when one does not accept it.
Gold has the principles of accepting and
not accepting,
and a dwelling should also have the principles of accepting and
not accepting.
Now, instead of saying
"I have no merit,"
or something like
"I have already retired and
accepting a dwelling would be unreasonable,"
he says
"I am not greedy for wealth and rank,"
using his previous refusal of ten *wàn* to exemplify his later refusal of one *wàn*.
Formerly, you were about to receive as many as one hundred thousand,
how could you decline it?
Péng Gēng asked,
"With dozens of chariots following behind,
and hundreds of followers,
taking food from the various feudal lords,
isn't that too extravagant?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"If it is not the right way,
then even a single basket of food should not be accepted from others;
if it is the right way,
then Shùn accepted the empire of Yáo,
and did not consider it excessive."
Accepting the empire of Yáo,
what compares to one hundred thousand?
The reason Shùn did not decline the empire,
was because it was the right way.
Now, instead of saying
"Accepting one hundred thousand is not the right way,"
but saying
"I am not greedy for wealth and honor,"
you have lost your humility and modesty,
how can this serve as a warning?
Shěn Tóng privately asked,
"Is it permissible to attack Yān?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"It is permissible.
Zǐ Kuài
and Zǐ Zhī was not allowed to receive Yān from Zǐ Kuài.
Suppose there were a scholar here,
and you were pleased with him,
and without informing the king, you privately gave him the rank and emolument of Zǐ Zhī.
If that scholar,
without the king's command, privately accepted them from you,
would that be permissible?
How is this different from that?"
The people of Qí attacked Yān.
Someone asked:
"Did you encourage Qí to attack Yān?"
He replied:
"No.
Shěn Tóng said:
'Is Yān worth attacking?'
I replied to him, saying:
'Yes!'
He then attacked it.
If he had said:
'Who can attack it?'
Then I would have replied, saying:
'One who is a minister of Heaven can attack it.'
Now, if someone is committing murder,
and someone asks you:
'Is it permissible to kill a person?'
Then he would have responded,
"Yes!"
If he then said,
"Who can kill him?"
then he would have responded,
"One who is a *shìshī* (士師, officer of justice) can kill him."
Now, using Yān to attack Yān,
why are you encouraging it?"
Someone asked if Mèngzǐ (孟子) encouraged the king to attack Yān.
Isn't that true?
Shěn Tóng (沈同) asked if Yān could be attacked.
This was harboring a private intention to attack it himself.
Knowing that his intention was satisfied with this,
it would have been appropriate to say,
"Although Yān can be attacked,
one must be an official of Heaven
before one can attack it."
If Shěn Tóng's (沈同) intention was cut off,
then there would be no plan to attack Yān.
Not knowing that he had this private intention and directly responding to him,
not examining his words,
is not knowing language.
Gōngsūn Chǒu (公孫丑) asked,
"May I ask what your strength lies in, Master?"
Mèngzǐ (孟子) said,
"I understand language."
He further asked,
"What is meant by 'knowing words'?"
He said:
"[Knowing] biased words means knowing what they obscure;
lascivious words means knowing what they ensnare;
deviant words means knowing what they deviate from;
evasive words means knowing where they are exhausted.
If it originates in the heart,
it will harm the government;
if it is expressed in the government,
it will harm affairs.
Even if a sage were to rise again,
he would surely follow my words."
Mèngzǐ,
is one who knows words,
and also knows the harm that arises from words,
and the ultimate harm they can lead to.
Seeing their question,
then he knows what their choice of words intends,
knowing where it goes,
then knows where it should ultimately harm.
Mèngzǐ once said:
"The people are restless,

When there are clouds, there is rain;
when there is rain, there are clouds.
Initially, it emerges as clouds,
when the clouds thicken, it becomes rain.
Similar to heavy dew and moisture soiling clothes,
resembling the appearance of rain.
It is not carried along with clouds,
the clouds do not carry the rain.
Someone asked:
"The *Shàngshū*
'When the moon follows the stars,
then there will be wind and rain.'
The [Shī] says:
'When the moon is attached to the Bì constellation,
there will be heavy rain.'
Both classics say the same thing.
What is called 'caused by something other than Heaven,' what does it mean?"
Now, rain originates from mountains.
The moon passing through and being attached to the Bì constellation,
when the moon is attached to the Bì constellation, it should rain.
When the time arrives, but it doesn't rain,
the moon isn't attached,
the mountain doesn't produce clouds,
the heavens and the earth above and below naturally correspond with each other.
The moon is attached above,
the mountain steams below,
When atmospheric elements happen to combine,
it is the natural way.
Clouds and mist
are signs of rain.
In summer they become dew,
in winter they become frost,
when warm they become rain,
when cold they become snow.
Rain, dew, freezing and congealing
all arise from the earth,
It does not descend from Heaven.
"Answering Flattery"
Someone asked:
"When the worthy practice the Way,
they obtain honored positions and generous salaries; why
must people resort to flattery to acquire wealth and status?"
He replied:
"The flatterer knows that practicing the Way can obtain wealth and status,
but they necessarily take rank and emolument through flattery
because they cannot restrain their desires.
They know that diligent farming can obtain grain,
and striving in trade can obtain goods,
yet they necessarily steal and rob,
because their emotions and desires cannot be restrained.
Advancing and retreating according to propriety
is something everyone values,
yet those who violate propriety are many,
and those who honor righteousness are few,
because their minds are greedy and lustful,
and their intentions and considerations are confused and drowned.
Now, flatterers and the worthy possess the same talents,
but flatterers ruin themselves through emotions;
thieves and farmers/merchants have the same knowledge,
but thieves indict themselves through desires."
He asked:
"Flatterers and the worthy possess the same talents,
and their talents and conduct should be equal,
so why do flatterers alone ruin themselves through emotions?"
He replied:
"Wealth and status are what everyone desires,
and even with the conduct of a gentleman,
there are still feelings of hunger and thirst."
The gentleman is able to use propriety to restrain his emotions
and righteousness to curtail his desires,
therefore he is able to follow the correct path.
Following the correct path results in no misfortune.
The petty man indulges his greedy desire for profit,
transgressing propriety and violating righteousness.
Therefore, he can advance through deceitful flattery.
Deceitful flattery results in crime.
Now, the virtuous are
gentlemen,
and flatterers are
petty men.
Gentlemen and petty men inherently have different principles and divergent conduct,
with different things they choose to take and reject."
Someone asked:
"Do flatterers and slanderers follow the same path?
Are there differences between them?"
He replied:
"Slanderers and flatterers
are both petty men.
They follow the same path but have different abilities.
Both are inherently driven by jealousy,
but their actions and machinations differ.
Slanderers harm people with their mouths,
flatterers endanger people through their actions.
Slanderers do not deviate from straightforward paths,
flatterers equivocate and conceal their motives.
Slanderers are without deceitful scheming,
flatterers possess cunning tactics.
Therefore, rulers are generally able to distance themselves from slanderers and be close to the benevolent,
but none can truly discern the worthy and distinguish them from the flatterers.
A question arises:
"If rulers are generally able to distance themselves from slanderers and be close to the benevolent,
but none can truly discern the worthy and distinguish them from flatterers,
then is the intention of the flatterer unknowable?"
I respond:
"Flatterers can be known,
but rulers are unable to know them.
Mediocre rulers
cannot know the worthy;
being unable to know the worthy,
they cannot know the flatterers.
Only the sage and the wise
use the nine virtues to examine their conduct,
and use the results of their actions to verify their words.
If conduct does not accord with the nine virtues,
and words are not validated by the results of their actions,
then the person is either not worthy or is a flatterer.
Knowing the flatterer comes from knowing the worthy,
and knowing the worthy comes from knowing the flatterer.
knowing the deceitful causes the virtuous and wise to be self-aware;
and knowing the worthy exposes the treachery of the villainous.
The worthy and the flatterer have different actions;
examining them with a single test
their true hearts differ."
observing them yields a concrete understanding.
Someone asks:
"The method of the Nine Virtues
has been established for a long time.
Those who read and study it
all understand and see it clearly,
like knowing the quantity of a *dǒu* and *hú*,
or the weight measured by scales.
Yet why do rulers who govern a state and possess land constantly have wicked and deceitful ministers,
and constantly suffer from the trouble of being deceived?"
I reply:
"The problem is not the lack of *dǒu* and *hú*;
it is that what is being measured is not the proper grain.
The problem is not the lack of scales;
it is that what is being weighed is not the proper object."
Those who sit in the position of ruler
all know that the Nine Virtues can be used to examine behavior,
and that the effectiveness of actions can reveal intentions,
but the reason they are unable to see through confusion
is that their discernment is not thorough.
There are people who are unable to act,
but no action cannot be examined.
There are people who are unable to be tested,
but no intention cannot be known.
Someone asks:
"If conduct does not conform to the Nine Virtues,
one's achievements are not examined by the ministry of evaluation,
those promoted are close (to power) and not worthy,
if they are not worthy, then they are sycophants.
Regarding those of mediocre talent,
lacking superior knowledge, unable to reach the level of the worthy,
the meritorious achievements of the worthy are not apparent,
can they be called sycophants?"
He replies:
"Talents are not mutually equal,
conduct is not mutually identical,
achievements are not mutually inherited.
If one knows that (achievements) are not mutually inherited,
and that talents and abilities differ by tenfold or a hundredfold,
acceptance or rejection should be similar.
The worthy and sycophants have different conduct;
the conduct of the worthy is not followed,
what is right is right, and what is wrong is wrong;
the actual substance and reputation should be both established.
However, achievements have success and failure,
the words of right and wrong are both appropriate;
accomplishments have righteousness and evil;
words agree (with the times) but actions deviate,
When reputation flourishes and practice declines,
it is due to flattering people.
Someone asked:
"If conduct aligns with the nine virtues, then one is virtuous;
if it does not align, then one is a flatterer.
Can all those who conduct themselves in the world be called flatterers?"
I replied:
Not all who are wrong are evil;
among the evil, those who are rebellious
are called unprincipled;
among the evil, those who are cunning
are called flatterers.
In the penal laws of the sagely kings,
flattery lies within evil;
in the rewards and encouragements of the sagely kings,
virtue lies within good.
Pure and flawless virtue
is exceptionally high within goodness;
it is the sage among the virtuous.
Great flattery within evil
is the most formidable among the evil.
Therefore, it is said:
"Observe virtue through goodness,
discern flattery through evil."
Once good and evil are definitively established,
the forms of virtue and flattery are revealed.
Someone asked:
"Intelligence has its limitations,
and implementation can have errors.
If we now regard those who are right as virtuous
and those who are wrong as flatterers,
we might not obtain the true essence of virtue, might we?"
I replied:
and promotion can have errors.
Zé Qín wèi ér liù guó qiáng; [If] then Qín would fear and the six states would be strong;
sān Qín chēng héng, [If] the Three Qins claimed hegemony,
zé Qín qiáng ér tiānxià ruò. [then] Qín would be strong and the world weak.
Gōng zhù xiào míng, Achievement manifested, effect evident,
zài jì zhú bó, recorded on bamboo and silk,
suī xián hé yǐ jiā zhī? even a worthy person could not surpass it.
Tàishǐgōng xù yán zhòng xián, The Grand Historian's narrative praises many worthies,
Yí, Qín yǒu piān, Yí and Qín have chapters [dedicated to them],
wú jí è zhī wén, without words of criticism,
gōng jūn míng dí, their achievements were comparable, their reputations matched,
bù yì yú xián. not different from the worthy.
Fú gōng zhī bù kěyǐ xiào xián, Now, achievements cannot be compared to worthiness,
yóu míng zhī bù kě shí yě. just as reputation cannot be equated to reality.
Yí, Qín, Yí and Qín,
pái nán zhī rén yě, were men who overcame difficulties,
chù rǎorǎng zhī shì, living in turbulent times,
xíng chuǎimó zhī shù, practicing the art of speculation,
dāng cǐ zhī shí, at that time,
Jì, Qì bù néng yǔ zhī zhēng jì, Jì and Qì could not compete with them in schemes,
Yǔ, Gāoyáo bù néng yǔ zhī bǐ xiào. Yǔ and Gāoyáo could not match them in effectiveness.
Ruòfú yīnyáng tiáohé, As for the Yin and Yang being in harmony,
fēngyǔ shí shì, timely wind and rain,
wǔgǔ fēng shú, abundant harvests of the five grains,
dàozéi shuāi xī, decline in thieves and robbers,
rén jǔ lián ràng, people promoting honesty and yielding,
jiā xíng dàodé zhī gōng, families practicing the achievements of morality and virtue,
mìnglù guì měi, noble and beautiful fate and fortune,
shùshù suǒ zhì, are brought about by numerological arts,
It is not accomplished through immorality.
The Grand Historian (Tàishǐ Gōng) recorded achievements,
therefore the merits were lofty and far-reaching.
The records were completed, then
the effects and clear proofs were demonstrated.
He encompassed and recorded the outstanding,
because Yí and Qín had meritorious achievements,
therefore he listed their deeds.
Judging from this,
flatterers can also establish merit and produce effects through power and persuasion.
Without effect,
one cannot be a flatterer.
Objection:
"Those who establish merit through wickedness are called flatterers.
Those who are able to achieve merit
are highly talented and knowledgeable.
Those who think deeply and far-sightedly
must rely on righteousness and depend on benevolence,
excelling among great worthies.
Therefore, the chapter "Awakening to Flatterers" says:
'If the ruler loves debate,
flatterers speak of profit;
if the ruler loves literature,
flatterers use ornate language.'
Hearts and minds aligning,
fortuitously pleasing the ruler,
speaking without their faults being seen,
how can one know their falsehood and watch for their treachery?"
Said:
This describes a mediocre (yōngyōng) ruler,
with talent that is low and understanding that is dim,
obscured by delusions, unable to see clearly.
A worthy and sagacious (xiánshèng) ruler
examines things with careful clarity,
as if looking at dried meat on a chopping board,
or tracing the lines in the palm of one's hand,
or counting chess pieces on a game board,
or selecting a horse from within an enclosure.
When fish and turtles hide in the deep,
fishermen know their hiding place;
when birds and beasts conceal themselves in the mountains,
hunters discern their trails.
When flatterers behave strangely in the world,
the world cannot see it.
With a mediocre (yōngyōng) ruler,
there are no people of high talent.
Someone objects (nàn):
"If a ruler enjoys debate,
flatterers will speak of profit;
if a ruler enjoys literature,
flatterers will use elegant language.
Their words and actions are in agreement;
How can one become aware of them?"
Said:
The *Wén Wáng Guān Rén Fǎ* 文王官人法 ("The Method of Employing Men by King Wén") says:
"Examine their past actions to evaluate their present words;
Listen to his present words to examine his past deeds.
Observe his outward actions to investigate his hidden intentions.
Therefore, those who deceitfully feign goodness and establish artificial propriety can be known.
Those who adorn themselves with falseness and lack genuine feeling can be distinguished.
Those who are genuinely sincere and dwell in goodness can be found.
Examine his inner self to measure his outer behavior.
Those who harbor loyalty and uphold integrity can be seen."
If people's true nature is not discerned,
and the ruler delights in clever arguments,
then flatterers will learn to seek to please the ruler.
If people's inherent abilities are unadorned,
and the ruler delights in embellishment,
then flatterers will intend to imitate the ruler.
If the ruler is extravagant,
then they will wear splendid clothes.
If the ruler is frugal,
then they will not adorn themselves.
Nowadays, conduct differs from the ancients,
and behavior in court differs from behavior at home.
Examine traces of behavior in the village,
verify conduct in the court,
observe integrity with shared relatives,
clarify faithfulness in serving the ruler.
If outer appearance and inner reality do not match,
if reputation and substance do not correspond,
then when the opportune moment arrives, the treachery will be exposed.
Someone asked:
"People's conduct is not constant.
They adapt to the times and circumstances.
The trustworthy deceive others.
The upright bend and yield.
Due to expedient changes,
conduct differs before and after.
matters are responded to variably,
words differ to the left and right.
The *Rú* scriptures record
that expedient changes are not uniform.
If we now examine them based on their original state,
wouldn't that be missing the point?"
He replied:
"The virtuous have expediency,
the flatterers have expediency.
When the virtuous have expediency,
there is a fitting outcome;
when the flatterers have expediency,
it also goes against principle,
and there is a bad outcome.
Therefore, the expediency of the virtuous
is for the sake of affairs and the country;
the expediency of the flatterers
is for the sake of themselves and their families.
Observe what they use expediency for,
and the virtuous and flatterers can be distinguished;
examine their motivations,
and what is wicked and upright can be named."
Someone asked:
"Flatterers like to slander people,
is this true?"
I replied:
Flatterers do not slander people.
If they slander people,
they are slanderers.
Why?
Flatterers seek profit,
therefore they do not slander people.
If it benefits themselves,
why would they slander others?
If it does not benefit themselves,
slandering them is of no use.
They calculate to seek advantage,
they use numbers to obtain profit,
if there is profit, then advantage is gained.
They are jealous of people who share the same work,
and then endanger them.
When they endanger people, it is not through slander;
and when they harm people, it is not openly.
They endanger people by praising them,
so people do not realize it;
they harm people through generosity,
so people do not suspect them.
Therefore, when flatterers endanger people, people are endangered without complaint;
when they harm people, people are ruined without resentment,
Ǐnqíng nìyì
is considered a skill.
If you slander others,
they will also slander you.
If you are not close to the masses,
and scholars do not attach themselves to you,
how can you gain acceptance in the world and obtain benefits from above?
Someone asked:
"Do flatterers not slander people in the world,
but slander them before the general?"
It is said:
Flatterers deceive the general with people,
they do not slander people before the general.
"Then what do flatterers do?"
It is said:
Flatterers slander people,
while praising them;
they endanger people,
while pacifying them.
How is someone slandered while endangered?
For example, if Jiǎ
has noble conduct and extraordinary wisdom, his reputation is widely known,
and the general fears that the ruler will summon him for questioning,
supporting him and surpassing himself,
he deliberately neglects to speak of him,
while constantly praising him.
If many recommend him,
and the general intends to employ him,
Asking about a flatterer;
the flatterer will surely answer,
"Jiǎ (甲) is virtuous and should be summoned.
Why?
Jiǎ's (甲) intention is not to remain in the county;
I have previously heard him say so.
His reputation aims to enter the prefecture,
and in the district, he hopes to enter the province.
If his ambition is high, his conduct will differ from others;
if he looks far ahead, his intentions will not consider what is near.
If you condescend to employ him,
his heart will not be satisfied,
or he will feign illness.
If you appoint him while he is lowly, it will injure his virtue,
or it will diminish your authority.
Therefore, the reason why a ruler loses his reputation and damages his honor
is that he favors ministers whom other rulers always favor.
If you can bear to humble yourself before him,
employing him is acceptable;
if you believe you cannot humble yourself before him,
employing him is inconvenient.
If employing him does not benefit both sides,
dismissing him does not harm both sides."
The ruler fears his ambition
and believes the flatterer's words,
and thus decides not to employ him.
Asking,
“Do flattering people directly use their high talent and vast knowledge to examine the people of ancient times?
Or do they have teachers and learning to guide them?”
He replied:
"Flattering people have their own intelligence to deceive people.
When they persuade the ruler,
they must use strategies to move the superior,
just as superior people have their own courage to intimidate people,
but when they fight,
they must use military tactics to advance the masses.
The strategies come from the school of diplomacy (Zònghéng),
and their teacher is Guǐ Gǔzi."
The *Commentary* says:
"Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí learned the art of diplomacy from Guǐ Gǔ xiānshēng.
They dug a pit in the ground, saying:
'Descend,
and if your persuasion makes me weep,
then you are capable of dividing the land of a ruler.'
Sū Qín descended,
and his words caused Guǐ Gǔ xiānshēng to weep until his lapel was soaked.
Zhāng Yí was not as good."
Sū Qín became the prime minister of Zhào,
and also served as prime minister of the six states concurrently.
Zhāng Yí was poor and humble
and went to return to Sū Qín.
Sū Qín made him sit below the hall,
fed him with the food of servants and concubines,
repeatedly reproached and provoked him,
wanting to make him become the prime minister of Qín.
Yí, filled with resentment,
subsequently went west and entered Qín.
Sū Qín had someone give him a generous send-off.
Later, he realized
and said,
"This was within his scheme,
I did not know it.
This is where I am inferior to Sū Jūn."
Knowing that he was deeply skilled,
his expedient plans were sharp and emergent,
therefore his person was honored, revered, and prominent,
becoming an outstanding figure of the age.
Deep planning and clear methods,
depth and shallowness cannot go hand in hand,
clarity and obscurity cannot be known at the same time.
Someone asked:
"Do sycophants cultivate a reputation and act lofty,
is that so?"
They replied:
"Sycophants seek profit and monopolize power,
they do not cultivate a reputation and act lofty.
Greedily seizing power and dominating everything,
then a lofty reputation will establish itself.
It is praised among petty people,
but not practiced by gentlemen.
Why?
Profit and righteousness attack each other,
Righteousness and wickedness are opposites.
Righteousness moves the noble person,
profit moves the petty person.
If a flattering person greedily seeks fame and prominence,
the ruler will not be at peace. Otherwise, his person will be in danger.
If the whole world becomes flatterers,
they will all bring disaster to the masses.
If one cannot nourish one's own body,
how can one nourish one's reputation?
The biographies of past generations record: abandoning clan to nourish the body,
forsaking profit to pursue fame.
What is recorded on bamboo and silk
is that Bóchéng Zǐgāo 伯成子高 relinquished his state to till the land,
and Yúlíng Zǐ 於陵子 resigned his position to water his garden.
In recent times, Lánlíng Wáng Zhòngzǐ 蘭陵王仲子,
and Dōngjùn Xīlú Jūnyáng 東郡昔廬君陽
remained sick in their beds for a long time,
and did not respond to the emperor's summons;
they can be said to have nourished their reputation.
If one does not advance by the proper way,
one will certainly not withdraw by the proper way;
if one does not stop for righteousness,
one will certainly not establish a reputation for righteousness.
Flatterers harbor greedy hearts,
regard misfortune lightly and their bodies highly,
so they will be disgraced even in death.
How can this be nourishing one's reputation?
When righteousness is abandoned and virtue is ruined,
When conduct follows disgrace,
how can one claim to be lofty?
Someone asked:
"Is it easy to recognize a great sycophant?
Or is it easy to recognize a small sycophant?"
Answer:
It is easy to recognize a great sycophant,
but difficult to recognize a small sycophant.
Why is this so?
A great sycophant has high talent,
and their traces are easily observed.
A small sycophant only knows how to work below,
and their effects are difficult to examine.
How can this be explained?
In achieving things:
a small thief is hard to detect,
but a great thief is easy to know.
Attacking cities and raiding settlements,
plundering and pillaging,
once it happens, the matter is known,
and everyone knows it is theft.
But tunneling through walls,
creeping like foxes and stealing like mice,
no one knows who it is.
Someone said:
"The deceit of a great sycophant is deep, misleading the ruler.
If a great sycophant were easy to recognize,
what difficulty would a ruler have?
The *Book of Documents* says:
"To know men is wisdom;
even Emperor is troubled by it."
Yú Shùn was a great sage,
Huān Dōu was a great villain.
For a great sage to know a great villain is difficult,
for a great villain not to worry about a great sage is easy,
how could it be easy?"
It is said:
"This refers to knowing it from below,
knowing it from above."
Knowing it from above, the great is difficult, the small is easy;
knowing it from below, the great is easy, the small is difficult.
Why is this?
Great villains have high talent,
their arguments and explanations are elegant and beautiful.
Because of the elegant and beautiful arguments,
and the majesty of the ruler,
people's determination is unable to censure them,
knowledge sometimes cannot perceive them.
Small villains have low talent,
they make mistakes and omissions towards the village,
their scheming is not discreet,
the ruler is alert and perceptive,
and can understand the reasons for their actions.
This is why the great is difficult and the small is easy.
A leak in the house is at the top,
those who know are at the bottom.
A large leak
is clearly visible below;
a small leak
is only subtly visible below.
Someone said:
"Yōng yě is benevolent but not eloquent."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"What use is eloquence?
To defend oneself with clever words
often incurs the hatred of the people."
Flawed planning and calculations,
vexing and disturbing farmers and merchants,
harming the lower classes to benefit the upper classes,
causing the people to grieve while pleasing the ruler.
Harming the upper classes to benefit the lower classes
is the talk of a loyal minister;
harming the lower classes to benefit the upper classes
is the conduct of a flatterer.
"[The Jì family] is richer than the Duke of Zhōu,
and Qiú yě collects taxes and increases their wealth for them.
The disciples may beat the drum and attack him.
In collecting taxes,
the Jì family does not know its wickedness,
does not know that it is universally condemned by the people."
_Chéng Cái Piān_ (Assessing Talents Chapter)
Many commentators say that Confucian scholars are not as good as those clerical officials,
seeing clerical officials as efficient and convenient, and Confucian scholars as slow and unsuccessful,
Then they criticize Rúshēng 儒生 scholars as being shallow and short-sighted,
and praise clerical officials (wénlì 文吏) as being profound and far-reaching.
This shows that they do not understand Rúshēng 儒生,
and also do not understand clerical officials (wénlì 文吏).
Both Rúshēng 儒生 and clerical officials (wénlì 文吏) possess talent and intelligence.
It is not that clerical officials (wénlì 文吏) are more talented and Rúshēng 儒生 are less intelligent.
Clerical officials (wénlì 文吏) have more experience in practical matters,
which Rúshēng 儒生 have not learned.
To say that clerical officials (wénlì 文吏) have more experience in practical matters
and that Rúshēng 儒生 have not learned this
is acceptable.
But to say that clerical officials (wénlì 文吏) are profound and far-reaching
and Rúshēng 儒生 are shallow and short-sighted
is knowingly false.
The common people generally disparage Rúshēng 儒生,
and even Rúshēng 儒生 themselves look down on each other.
Why is this?
Because they all admire officialdom and pursuing an official career,
using clerical officials (lì 吏) as their standard and model.
When Rúshēng 儒生 have shortcomings,
the common people all criticize them;
when clerical officials (wénlì 文吏) make mistakes,
the common people do not dare to censure them.
They attribute faults to Rúshēng 儒生
and give credit to clerical officials (wénlì 文吏).
The talent of Rúshēng 儒生 is not inferior to that of clerical officials (wénlì 文吏),
and the studies they have pursued are not unrelated to what they should be doing.
However, the common people generally criticize them,
seeing that the generals are not good at employing people.
The generals who are not good at employing people
often find that they cannot manage many affairs themselves
and must rely on clerical officials (wén lì) to oversee them.
Now, the point of discussing good planning and talent,
employing them to accumulate abilities,
is to aim for benefit.
Clerical officials manage complex matters,
personally dedicating themselves to their duties;
when duties are judged and achievements established,
the generals respect their abilities.
Confucian scholars (rú shēng) are timid and apprehensive,
unable to handle difficult situations;
when generals have troubles and doubts,
they cannot provide effective assistance.
If their efforts are of no benefit to the times,
then official positions will not reach them.
If generals evaluate talent based on official positions,
and talent is proven by official positions,
therefore the common people often value clerical officials highly
and look down upon Confucian scholars.
The inferiority of Confucian scholars
and the superiority of clerical officials
fundamentally arise from incompetent generals.
The opinions of the common people
are based on the likes and dislikes of the generals.
Nowadays, generals
possess high talent and profound knowledge,
are versed in all matters,
grasp the main principles and maintain control,
and nothing remains undecided.
As for their appointment of civil officials,
they merely fill the required quota,
sufficient to assist their own will.
If their will is focused on cultivating virtue
and their effort is on establishing moral influence,
then those civil officials are mere tiles and stones,
while the Confucian scholars are pearls and jade.
Civil officials are capable of breaking through difficulties and managing complex affairs,
but are unable to preserve their integrity.
[Unable to preserve] their integrity
then they are also unable to assist the general.
Confucian scholars are not skilled in their duties,
but excel at correction and rescue.
When generals and ministers are leaning towards ruin,
they fearlessly offer difficult remonstrances.
Examining
the world, those who can establish unwavering integrity [jiǎn jiǎn zhī jié],
accomplish the counsel of "three remonstrances" [sān jiàn zhī yì],
cause the general to examine himself and be self-disciplined [jiǎn shēn zì chì],
and dare not be wicked or devious,
are mostly Confucian scholars.
Those who curry favor and seek fortune,
are about to abandon propriety and lose their way,
Those who are silent and do not speak out freely,

A scholar who practices and is refined in learning,
and who matures under a teacher,
benefits himself,
like grain becoming cooked rice,
eating it creates muscle and plumpness.
Copper and tin that have not been mined
are among many rocks.
Craftsmen chisel and dig,
and smelt them in furnaces with bellows to make utensils.
Before they have been through the furnace and bellows,
they are called accumulated stones (jī shí).
Accumulated stones are the same as the tiles by the roadside and the gravel in the mountains.
Therefore, grain that has not been husked and steamed is called unhusked millet.
Copper that has not been cast and smelted is called accumulated stones.
A person who has not learned is called ignorant (méng).
The ignorant (méng),
are like bamboo and wood.
Now, bamboo grows on mountains,
and trees grow in forests;
their ultimate use is unknown.
Bamboo is cut into tubes,
split into slips,
and marked with traces of brush and ink,
thus forming writing.
The large ones become *jīng* (classics),
and the small ones become biographies (*zhuànjì*).
Wood is cut into blocks (*qiàn*),
split into boards,
and forcefully scraped and smoothed,
thus becoming memorials (*zòudú*).
Bamboo and wood
are coarse and rough materials,
but through carving and shaping,
they become useful implements.
How much more so are humans, who possess the nature of Heaven and Earth,
and are the most noble of beings!
If one does not enter the teacher's gate
and receive the teachings of the classics and commentaries,
remaining in their uncultivated state,
without understanding propriety and righteousness,
then placing them in the court
is like planting stakes and marker posts –
what benefit is there?
In the mountains and fields, grass grows luxuriantly;
with sickle and scythe it is cut down,
Thus, a road is formed.
Before a scholar enters the gate of the Dao,
and evil is not yet removed,
he is like wild grass and trees in the mountains that have not been cut down,
and a road has not yet been formed.
Cloth that has been dyed and refined
is called *cǎi* (彩, colorful),
and is clothing suitable for auspicious occasions.
Without the work of dyeing and refining, it is called *hú cù* (觳麤, coarse cloth).
*Hú cù* is inauspicious;
mourners wear it.
If a person has no learning in the Dao
and serves as an official in the court,
the good fortune he cannot attract
is like a mourner wearing coarse cloth, unable to attract good fortune.
One who can carve pillars and beams
is called a carpenter;
one who can drill holes and dig pits
is called an earthworker;
one who can engrave documents
is called a scribe.
The learning of a civil official
is learning to manage documents.
It should be in the same category as the skills of carpenters and earthworkers.
How can it be compared to Confucian scholars?
When a censor encounters a document,
he doesn't lose a fraction of a *zhū* (銖, a weight unit).
The officials in charge arrange the biàn and dòu vessels
without making mistakes in their rows and columns.
Those who are skilled in these arts
also learn them first.
These are not the people who are esteemed;
it is a minor, humble skill,
not a position of great authority.
Lacking the foundation of classical learning,
but possessing the trivial skills of writing,
with the great Way not being sufficient, yet minor skills being in excess,
even if one says, "I have much learning,"
it is due to the additions of the censor and the favors of the officials.
Those who eat millet and sorghum are satiated,
those who eat dregs and chaff are full.
Though both are called eating,
the richness is different.
Confucian scholars and scribes,
both claim to have mastered their learning;
their benefit to the court
is not equal.
Zhèng Zǐpí appointed Yǐn Hé to govern;
Zǐchǎn compared it to being unable to hold a knife and yet being made to cut.
Zǐlù appointed Zǐ Gāo as the magistrate of Fèi;
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He is harming someone else's son."
All of this is because they had not learned and did not see the great Way.
A doctor without methods and techniques says:
"I can cure diseases."
Asked him, saying:
"What do you use to treat illness?"
He said:
"With intent and thought (xīnyì)."
The patient will surely not believe him.
An official without classical learning says:
"I can govern the people."
Asked him, saying:
"What do you use to govern the people?"
He said:
"With talent and ability (cáinéng)."
This is like a doctor without prescriptions
using intent and thought (xīnyì) to treat illness.
How could the common people willingly believe and follow him,
and would a ruler employ and use him?
Having no money in hand, one goes to the market
to negotiate a purchase. The seller asks:
"Where is the money?"
He replies:
"I have no money."
The seller will certainly not give it to him.
Having no learning in one's mind
is just like having no money in one's hand.
To want the ruler to employ and use him,
and the common people to believe and follow him, what can be done?
"Xiè Short Essay"
"Assessing Ability" and "Measuring Knowledge"
It is said that the talents of Confucian scholars and scribes cannot surpass each other.
This is because Confucian scholars cultivate the great Way,
while scribes are familiar with documents and records.
The Way is superior to practical matters.
Therefore, it is said that Confucian scholars are somewhat better than scribes.
This is an external comparison and measurement of their professions.
Internally, each has its own shortcomings.
This is not truly acknowledged.
A Confucian scholar who can expound on a single classic
considers himself to have mastered the great Way, and uses this to examine scribes.
A scribe who is familiar with documents and records
considers his writing to be harmless and uses this to mock Confucian scholars.
Each holds himself full and hides within himself,
affirming himself and denying the other.
They do not know their own shortcomings
and do not realize their own inadequacies.
*Lùn Héng* critiques them
in order to make them suddenly aware of their respective deficiencies.
The shortcoming of Confucian scholars
is not merely their unfamiliarity with documents and records.
The inferiority of scribes
is not merely their lack of understanding of the great Way.
It is rather their closed-mindedness and failure to study the past and present,
and their inability to recognize the incompleteness of their own professional knowledge.
Both have their shortcomings,
but neither can recognize them.
The world's critics,
are also unable to refute them,
why is this?
The profession of a Confucian scholar
is the Five Classics.
Facing south as a teacher,
morning and night, they lecture on phrases and sentences,
fluently practicing the meaning of principles,
thoroughly mastering the Five Classics,
that is acceptable.
After the Five Classics,
if the affairs of the Qín and Hàn dynasties
are something they are unable to know,
that is a shortcoming.
To know the past but not the present,
is called "sunken land" (lù chén).
In that case, the Confucian scholar
is what is called "sunken land."
Before the Five Classics,
going back to when heaven and earth first opened,
and the emperors first established themselves, whose names were they,
the Confucian scholar also does not know.
To know the present but not the past,
is called "blind and foolish" (máng gǔ).
Compared to high antiquity, the Five Classics
are still considered the present.
Merely being able to explain the classics,
but not understanding high antiquity,
Therefore, Confucian scholars are
what might be called blind men.
Confucian scholars still say:
"The ancient past is distant,
and its affairs are obscure,
therefore the classics do not record them, and teachers do not explain them."
Although the affairs of the Three Kings are indeed distant,
even if the classics do not record them,
the principles involved are connected,
and should be commonly known by those who study the Five Classics,
and carefully explained by Confucian scholars.
From Yǔ taking control of the Xia dynasty,
how many years until the Yin dynasty?
From Tāng of the Yin dynasty, how many years until the Zhou dynasty?
From King Wén of Zhou, how many years until the Qin dynasty?
Jié lost the Xia dynasty, and Zhòu abandoned the Yin dynasty,
which king destroyed the Zhou dynasty?
Zhou is still comparatively distant,
and Qin is what the Hàn dynasty overthrew.
Xia began with Yǔ,
Yin originated with Tāng,
and Zhou had Hòujì as its ancestor,
who was the first person to establish Qin?
Qin burned the Five Classics,
and buried Confucian scholars alive,
which is commonly heard of by those who study the Five Classics.
Why did Qin arise and burn the Five Classics?
Why did (they) feel the need to bury the Confucian scholars?
The Qín dynasty was a former dynasty.
The Hàn state is a family of Confucian scholars.
From Gāozǔ until the present dynasty, how many generations have there been?
How many years have passed until now?
What mandate was initially received?
What auspicious omens were subsequently obtained?
Compared to the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties, was obtaining the empire easy or difficult?
If one's family and children
have studied for several years,
and someone asks them:
"How many years have you lived in your residence?
What did your ancestors do?"
if they are unable to know (the answer),
they are foolish children.
If, therefore, Confucian scholars are unable to know the affairs of the Hàn dynasty,
they are foolish and ignorant people of the world.
To review the old and learn the new
is what it means to be a teacher.
If one does not know the past and present,
how can one be called a teacher?
That person said:
"Two chi and four cun
are the language of sages and men,
studied and practiced morning and evening.
The meaning and classification of things fall within their scope,
and therefore they should be diligently known.
Hàn affairs are not recorded in the classics;
It is called "ruler-measured short writings,"
comparable to minor skills.
That they are knowledgeable
is not something valued by Ru scholars."
Ru scholars cannot all understand ancient and modern matters.
They wish to separately explain their classics;
[regarding] matters, affairs, meanings, and categories,
they even consider ignorance to be valuable?
Not understanding matters
is not considered a shortcoming!
Please ask the Ru scholars again,
each according to their classic, what they lecture on morning and evening.
First ask the 《Yì》 (Book of Changes) experts:
"Where did the 《Yì》 originate?
Who created it?"
They will likely answer:
"Fúxī created the eight trigrams,
Wén Wáng expanded them into sixty-four,
and Kǒngzǐ wrote the Tuàn (Judgements), Xiàng (Images), and Xìcí (Appended Remarks).
The three sages accumulated their work,
and the 《Yì》 became complete."
Ask them:
"There are three schools of 《Yì》.

Was it Fúxī who created it,
What Wén Wáng 文王 created,

He asked the scholars of the *Lǐ* 禮 (Book of Rites):

all three kings
added or subtracted according to the times,

I don't know if the current *Lǐ* (Rites/Rituals)

Yīn, and Xià Dynasties?"

three hundred and sixty,

The sixteen chapters that exist now

During the time of the Qín Dynasty,
How many sections are there in a chapter?
Asking the *Shī* scholars:

At this time there was already poetry.

Ritual speaks of classic ritual,

If asked something simple,

The "Measuring Merit" chapter,
The chapters "Chéng Cái" and "Liàng Zhī"
merely speak of knowledge through learning,
and do not discuss talent and ability.
If a person has knowledge through learning,
then they have ability.
Clerical officials use managing affairs as their ability,
while Confucian scholars use learning as their ability.
Someone asked Yáng Zǐyún:

does he also have knowledge of virtue?"
He replied:
"Hundreds of people do."
To have knowledge of virtue possessed by hundreds is
comparable to lifting great cauldrons and raising flowered banners.
For strong men, abundant strength means
lifting cauldrons and raising banners;
for Confucian scholars, abundant strength means
broad understanding and clear communication.
Therefore, broad understanding and clear communication
are the strength of Confucian scholars;
lifting heavy objects and uprooting firm things

The "Zǐ Cái" chapter of the *Book of Documents* says:

This means that virtuous men are also strong in ritual and righteousness,
thus they can open up sagacity
They lead and transform the people.
Transforming the people requires ritual and righteousness;
ritual and righteousness require literature.
"If, in your practice, you have more than enough energy,

Being able to learn literature
is proof of having extra energy.
Someone asked:

He replied:
"He is not someone with extra energy."
Chénliú Páng Shǎodū, whenever he recommended local scholars as officials,

"Wáng Jiǎ, the son of so-and-so, has the talent of a hundred men."
The governor did not recognize his ability

Wáng Jiǎ, the son of so-and-so,

The governor angrily said:

Shǎodū said:

a scholar, being able to speak a million phrases and sentences,
“Is it not that one's talent and knowledge are equal to those of a million people?”
The governor had nothing to say in response.
Now, the words of Shǎo Dū
were true,
yet still not enough.
Why?
Because students can transmit a million words,
but cannot survey the past and present;
they adhere to the teachings of their masters,
and though their words are numerous,
they ultimately do not achieve broad knowledge.
The events before the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties

which Confucian students can explain.
But the affairs of the Qín and Hàn dynasties
are not seen by Confucian students;
their strength is insufficient to survey them.
The Zhōu dynasty learned from the two preceding dynasties,

The events since the Zhōu and Qín dynasties
are unknown to Confucian students.
If the Hàn dynasty wishes to survey them,
the Confucian students lack the ability.
If Confucian students could broadly survey and examine,
then they would become learned Confucians.
Learned Confucians
have more ability than regular Confucian students.
According to Shǎo Dū's words,
Wénrú's (文儒) talents are worth ten million people.
Zēngzǐ (曾子) said:
"A scholar cannot be without breadth of mind and resolute endurance,

To regard benevolence as his own burden,
is it not heavy?
To stop only after death,

From this saying,
what a Confucian scholar cherishes
is uniquely heavy;
what his ambition desires to reach
is uniquely far;
his body carries a heavy burden,
until death,
without weariness or decline,
his strength is uniquely abundant.
Zēngzǐ (曾子) carried benevolence, and Confucian students carry learning;
what they carry is different,
but the weight is the same.
Now, the weight of one *shí* (石, a unit of weight)
can be carried by one person;
but ten *shí* or more
cannot be lifted by two people.
The world is full of those who carry the burden of one *shí*,
but few have the strength to lift ten *shí*.

I say:
This is another suspicion.

*Míng Yú Piān* (Understanding Rain)
Families that have experienced reversal [of fortune],
consider prolonged rain to be inundation,
and prolonged sunshine to be drought.
Drought corresponds to excessive *yáng*,
and inundation corresponds to drowning.
Someone might object, saying:
"Within a year,
it rains once every ten days,
and the wind blows once every five days.
If the rain lingers somewhat,
it is a sign of inundation;
if the sunshine lasts somewhat longer,
it is a gradual sign of drought.
In times of inundation,
the ruler is not necessarily drowning in vice;
in times of drought,
he is not necessarily excessively *yáng*.
If the ruler's governance
is consistent throughout,
then occasional inundation and drought
are simply due to the season's *qì*."
The *Fàn Lǐ Jì Rán* says:
"When the Grand Year (Jupiter) is in Water, there will be destruction;
in Metal, abundance;
in Wood, famine;
in Fire, drought."
If this is so,
water, drought, famine, and abundance
are matters of the year's fortune.
The year directs its fortune,
the qi corresponds to its era,
and the families of change and restoration point to this and name it.
If the ruler uses their words
and seeks to correct his own faults,
prolonged sunshine will naturally turn to rain,
and prolonged rain will naturally turn to sunshine.
Then the families of change and restoration
will name it as their merit.
If the ruler approves of this,
he will believe in their methods.
But if the ruler lives peacefully and comfortably, not seeking his own faults,
the sky will still naturally rain,
and rain will still naturally turn to sunshine.
In times of sunshine alleviating rain or rain alleviating sunshine,
the ruler has nothing to do,
but the families of change and restoration
will still name it as their technique.
This would mean that the qi of yin and yang
is based on human action,
It does not accord with Heaven.
People cannot move Heaven with their actions;
Heaven does not respond to people based on their actions.

This is transformation and reversion.

The *Shū* (Book of Documents) says:
